2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern / Can't tell: Across the 100 villages, assessed household totals shifted slightly from n = 4699 in March 2012 to n = 4585 in March 2013 (Figure 1, Page 6; ~2.4% change, complicated by fluctuating joint-family reporting noted on Page 11). However, response/refusal rates for the 10% household survey (n = 807) and 10% VWSC member survey (n = 170) are not reported, village motivator turnover disrupted record continuity (Page 11), and village-level fidelity data were missing for 2 villages on VWSCs, 7 villages on mapping, and 13 villages on Kumari committees (Pages 4, 7).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Mixed (Low concern for randomized arm comparisons; High concern for within-arm ecological regressions): Comparisons of latrine construction progress (Figure 1) and awareness (Table 2) leverage the parent trial's 50:50 cluster randomization of 100 villages (balanced 8% baseline sanitation coverage; Page 4), though 49% of control households knew of the TSC via background exposure or spillover (Page 10). By contrast, the 13 village-level linear regressions within the 50 intervention villages (Table 4, Page 11) are non-randomized ecological analyses with zero adjustment for confounders (such as implementing NGO [coverage ranged 54%-76%], flood disruption in 13 villages, political unrest, or village poverty share).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: The paper accurately outlines the policy architecture and operational rules of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC, 1999) and its 2012 successor Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA), including BPL vs APL subsidy rules, the June 2011 subsidy increase from INR 2200 to INR 3200, Nirmal Gram Puraskar open-defecation-free incentives, VWSC mandates, and election code-of-conduct pauses (Pages 2-5, 9-10). Crucially, it empirically separates de jure TSC guidelines from de facto implementation (e.g., universalising subsidies to APL households via WaterAid funds to prevent village conflict, Page 7), though it cites administrative guidelines rather than primary statutory instruments.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Latrine construction status was measured rigorously through direct household inspection by independent enumerators every 6-8 weeks using explicit physical criteria (walls >1.5 m, door, unbroken/unblocked pan, functional pan-pipe-pit connection; Page 2), though assessors were unblinded and household denominators were distorted by joint families strategically over- or under-reporting splits depending on perceived subsidy benefits or cost contributions (Page 11). Mobilisation awareness relied on unvalidated self-report recall surveys (translated/back-translated into Oriya; Page 3), and delivery logs maintained by village motivators varied widely in completeness (Page 11).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-good for latrine construction; absent for actual latrine use: Physical latrine construction status ('completed' vs 'under construction'/damaged) was directly observed across households using clear structural specifications (Page 2), notwithstanding household-unit boundary difficulties in joint-family compounds (Page 11). Awareness and participation outcomes relied on retrospective self-report over 1-12 months. Despite the title referencing 'latrine construction and use', actual behavioural latrine use or open-defecation behaviour was not measured in this paper.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: The parent cluster-RCT was registered (NCT01214785) with a published design protocol [6], and the authors candidly report implementation shortfalls and largely null associations. However, no pre-analysis plan is cited for the process evaluation regressions, qualitative interviews with community members mentioned in Methods (Page 2) are not systematically reported in Results, and minor internal discrepancies appear between text and tables (Page 7 text cites p = 0.02 for motivator home visits in the past month whereas Table 4 reports p = 0.05; Table 2 prints count difference 230 instead of percentage difference for home visits and lists n = 257 NGO visitors out of n = 242 home-visit respondents).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: At the cluster level, 100 villages in Puri district were selected 'with government cooperation' (eligibility details deferred to protocol [6]) and randomly allocated 50:50 to intervention and control (Page 2). Within villages, the 10% household survey (n = 807) and 10% VWSC survey (n = 170) used random selection from village lists via Stata 13 (Pages 2-3), but sample sizes were based on logistical considerations, non-response/refusal rates are unreported, absent household heads were pragmatically substituted with any present household member aged >16 years (Page 2), and sampling for qualitative NGO/community interviews is not described.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The Methods section explicitly specifies four clear process evaluation objectives based on the Linnan and Steckler framework: documenting context, documenting intervention delivery, assessing target-population exposure, and exploring associations between mobilisation exposure and latrine construction.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Six longitudinal monitoring rounds in the 50 intervention villages (interviews with village motivators, NGO/VWSC logbook reviews, and direct household latrine observations), endline latrine observations across all 100 villages, and random-sample surveys of households (n = 807) and VWSC members (n = 170) directly address all four objectives.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining semi-structured interviews with implementing NGO staff, village motivators, and community members alongside documentary review of TSC guidelines, activity logbooks, meeting notes, and contribution/stock registers is well suited to documenting implementation context, delivery processes, and operational bottlenecks.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Although enumerators visited the 50 intervention villages every 6-8 weeks over six rounds to interview village motivators and inspect records, and interview guides were translated into Oriya and back-translated into English, the paper omits key qualitative collection details: it does not report sample sizes or recruitment for NGO-staff or community-member semi-structured interviews, whether interviews were audio-recorded or transcribed, or how incomplete motivator logbooks were handled when motivators left.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: While quantitative analysis in Stata 13 is specified, the paper provides zero description of how qualitative interview notes or documentary records were coded, synthesised, or analysed (e.g., no mention of thematic coding, analytic framework, or multiple coders), and presents no verbatim quotations from participants.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative interpretations regarding patchy mobilisation and implementation barriers are substantiated by concrete village-level counts from motivator interviews, document reviews, and direct field observations across the 50 intervention villages (e.g., documenting that half of the 37 villages reporting mapping merely had 2-3 VWSC members sketch a map on paper, why universal subsidies were adopted, and specific disruptions from the June 2011 subsidy change, road-project sand shortages, floods in 13 villages, and election pauses), triangulated with survey findings.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the Linnan and Steckler framework links qualitative sources to fidelity interpretation, full coherence cannot be verified because qualitative coding/analysis procedures are entirely unreported and semi-structured interviews with 'community members' mentioned in the Methods are never distinctly described or reported in the Results.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Latrine construction status was assessed via a census of households across all 50 intervention villages every 6-8 weeks (and all 100 trial villages at baseline and Jan-March 2013), while awareness and involvement surveys drew 10% simple random samples of households per village (50 intervention and 50 control villages) and 10% of VWSC members per village from complete lists using Stata 13's random generator, although sample sizes were determined by logistical considerations rather than formal power calculations.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: Random selection from village household and VWSC lists supports within-village representativeness, and baseline coverage (8%) is contextualised against Puri district (23%) and Orissa (15%) statistics; however, the 100 villages were selected 'with government cooperation' (criteria reported elsewhere [6]), absent household heads were pragmatically replaced by any present household member aged >16 years, and refusal/absence rates are unreported.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2-3, Methods and Study setting

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: Latrine construction was measured by direct physical inspection using explicit WaterAid structural specifications (walls >1.5 m, door, unbroken/unblocked pan, functional pan-pipe-pit connection), and Oriya questionnaires were back-translated into English; limitations openly noted include unvalidated recall items for mobilisation exposure, unblinded field enumerators, and household-unit boundary disputes among joint families strategically over- or under-reporting household counts.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: Participation, refusal, and replacement rates are not reported for either the 10% household survey (n = 807) or the 10% VWSC member survey (n = 170); additionally, process records were missing for 2 villages on VWSCs, 7 villages on mapping, and 13 villages on Kumari committees, and total assessed households changed from 4699 (March 2012) to 4585 (March 2013).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2-8, Methods and Results (Figure 1, Tables 2-3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: For intervention-versus-control comparisons (Table 2), comparing village-level proportions via Student's t-test appropriately accounts for village-level clustering. However, for Objective 4 (Table 4), the authors ran 13 separate unadjusted ecological linear regressions at the village level without controlling for village/NGO confounders or multiple testing, alongside minor text-table discrepancies (Page 7 text cites p = 0.02 for motivator home visit vs p = 0.05 in Table 4; Table 2 prints count difference 230 in a % column and n = 257 NGO visitors among n = 242 visited households). Overall statistical methods are broadly appropriate for descriptive/exploratory aims but limited for associational inference.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3, Methods; Pages 7-11, Results (Tables 2 and 4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Grounded in Linnan and Steckler's process evaluation framework [10], the authors clearly justify combining documentary review, qualitative interviews, direct physical observations, and structured surveys to distinguish the sanitation intervention as delivered from the intervention as planned.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration occurred both sequentially during instrument design (using guideline reviews and NGO interviews to build quantitative survey tools) and analytically in Results and Discussion by pairing qualitative accounts of village-level implementation with quantitative latrine coverage trajectories and household/VWSC awareness surveys.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2, Methods; Pages 4-11, Results and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Joint interpretation yields coherent substantive explanations—for instance, showing how qualitative reports of superficial or skipped PRA activities explain near-zero household recall of mapping (6%) and wealth ranking (0%), and how universalising subsidies to avoid community conflict produced comparable latrine coverage in BPL (68%) and APL (61%) households.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Divergences between planned TSC guidelines, NGO/motivator reports, and household survey recall (e.g., motivators reporting mapping in 37 villages vs 6% household recall; 49% TSC awareness in control villages; conflicting household counts between implementers and enumerators due to strategic reporting by joint families) are explicitly examined and explained.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: No: while integration and physical latrine inspections are strong, the qualitative component omits any description of coding/thematic analysis, community-interview sampling, or verbatim evidence and relies on uneven motivator logbooks, and the quantitative component omits survey response rates, lacks confounding control in village-level regressions (Table 4), and contains minor reporting inconsistencies in Tables 2 and 4.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2-3, Methods; Pages 7-11, Results and Discussion

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Boisson et al. (2014) report a mixed-methods process evaluation embedded within a 100-village cluster-randomised controlled trial of rural sanitation implemented under India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) in Puri district, Orissa. Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018; Screening S1-S2, Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative descriptive 4.1-4.5, and Mixed-Methods integration 5.1-5.5), the study demonstrates strong mixed-methods rationale, design integration, and triangulation (5.1-5.4 all 'Yes'), as well as rigorous longitudinal physical inspection of latrine construction by independent enumerators and valid cluster-level t-test comparisons of awareness across the 50 intervention and 50 control villages. However, per MMAT 2018 principles that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component, moderate methodological concerns arise (5.5 rated 'No'): the qualitative component provides no description of qualitative coding or analytic procedures, no verbatim quotes, unspecified sampling for community interviews, and incomplete NGO motivator logbooks (1.2, 1.3, 1.5 'Can't tell'); the quantitative surveys do not report non-response or refusal rates (4.2, 4.4 'Can't tell'); village-level linear regressions in Table 4 are unadjusted for confounders with minor text-table reporting discrepancies; household denominators were affected by strategic joint-family reporting around subsidies; and actual behavioural latrine use (as opposed to construction) was not measured.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (MMAT narrative judgment; overall quality constrained by weakest component: strong mixed-methods integration and objective latrine observation, but unreported qualitative coding/analysis, unreported survey response rates, incomplete motivator logs, and unadjusted ecological regressions)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Mixed-methods process evaluation conducted alongside a cluster-randomised controlled trial (combining qualitative semi-structured interviews and NGO/VWSC documentary reviews with longitudinal physical latrine observations, random-sample household and VWSC surveys, cluster-level arm comparisons, and village-level linear regressions)
raw_response.where_found_summary: PDF Pages 1-3 (Abstract and Methods: process evaluation objectives, 6-8 weekly monitoring rounds, physical latrine criteria, 10% random-sample household and VWSC surveys, Stata 13 village-level t-tests and linear regressions); Pages 3-11 (Results, Figures 1-2, Tables 1-4: context, TSC policy rules, fidelity, awareness, and coverage regressions); Pages 9-11 (Discussion: subsidy changes, floods, strategic household reporting, and incomplete motivator logbooks).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: While connected to a 100-village cluster-randomised trial whose design and health-impact evaluation are reported elsewhere [6], this paper itself is a primary mixed-methods process evaluation combining qualitative data (semi-structured interviews with NGO staff, village motivators, and community members plus documentary logbook/register reviews) and quantitative data (longitudinal household latrine observations, 10% random-sample surveys of households and VWSC members, cluster-level comparisons, and ecological linear regressions). MMAT (with the Quantitative descriptive 4.1-4.5 block alongside Qualitative 1.1-1.5 and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5) is therefore the exact matching instrument.
